policy.purpose: Evidence ledger for canonical Pattern Dictionary Wave 3 before any runtime publication.
policy.runtime_lock: data/patterns.json remains canonical 40 throughout this source-verification gate.
policy.primary_palette_rule: A fixed primary palette is an editorial recognition reference unless a source establishes color as identity-relevant. It is never presented as the only valid colorway.
policy.relationship_rule: similar and often_confused_with are visual-discovery relationships, not claims of shared historical origin unless explicitly sourced.
policy.qualification_rule: Use qualified when the term is fundamentally a form, weave, textile/style tradition, broad market/discovery label, or modern usage that does not resolve to one uniquely fixed motif.

patterns.structure: A continuous rectilinear line turns at right angles to form a repeated meander, commonly used as a border or band.

color_guidance.reason: The right-angled meander geometry carries recognition; color is not intrinsic to the motif.

patterns.structure: A symmetrical four-lobed figure with four rounded leaves or lobes separated by cusps.

color_guidance.reason: Recognition depends on the four-lobed outline rather than a fixed palette.

sources.publisher: Getty Research Institute, Art & Architecture Thesaurus

patterns.term_scope: ogee double-curve form used as a repeating surface-design family
patterns.structure: Opposed or interlocking S-shaped double curves repeat to create pointed, bulbous, or lozenge-like compartments.

color_guidance.reason: The double-curve silhouette is the recognition cue; color is not definitional.

patterns.qualification: Ogee is fundamentally an S-shaped or double-curved profile used in architecture and design, not one universal textile motif. Pattern Dictionary treats repeated opposed or interlocking ogee curves as a qualified surface-design family.

sources.publisher: Getty Research Institute, Art & Architecture Thesaurus

patterns.term_scope: generic crossed-strip or crisscross pattern family
patterns.structure: Crossing strips or lines form an open grid, commonly diagonal, with repeated spaces between the crossings.

color_guidance.reason: The crossed open-grid structure defines the visual family; color is variable.

patterns.structure: Adjacent six-sided cells repeat in a tightly packed cellular field resembling a bee honeycomb.

color_guidance.reason: Six-sided cellular repetition is structural; honey-like colors are only a recognition aid.

patterns.structure: Repeated rounded or fan-like semicircular arcs create overlapping rows or a wave-edged field reminiscent of scallop shells.

color_guidance.reason: The repeated rounded shell-like arcs carry recognition; palette is variable.

patterns.term_scope: weave structure and basket-like visual family
patterns.structure: Groups of two or more threads interlace as units, creating a blocky checked surface that resembles woven basket strips.

color_guidance.reason: Interlaced grouped structure is the key cue; natural basket colors are only illustrative.

patterns.qualification: Basketweave is a weave structure and visual effect, not one universal printed motif. The reference image may depict the interlaced basket-like appearance but must not imply one canonical thread count or construction.

sources.publisher: Museum of Fine Arts Boston, CAMEO

patterns.structure: Six-sided polygons repeat as isolated motifs, linked cells, or a tessellated field.

color_guidance.reason: The six-sided polygon geometry defines the pattern; color is variable.

patterns.structure: A repeated framework of intersecting or linked bands creates open compartments, which may be square, diamond, curved, or ornamented.

color_guidance.reason: The open framework/repeat structure is the cue; no one palette defines trellis patterns.

patterns.structure: Rhombus or diamond forms repeat singly or in linked arrangements; hishitsunagi is a connected-diamond variant.

color_guidance.reason: Rhombus geometry and Japanese motif context define recognition; indigo/white is illustrative only.

sources.publisher: JAANUS (Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System)

patterns.structure: A vertically symmetrical stylized flower commonly built from three principal petals or lobes, with the center rising above the side lobes.

color_guidance.reason: The stylized symmetric floral silhouette defines the motif; heraldic colorways vary.

sources.publisher: Getty Research Institute, Art & Architecture Thesaurus

patterns.term_scope: printed-textile/design tradition associated with pictorial figural scenes
patterns.structure: Pictorial figures, landscapes, pastoral or narrative scenes are printed across a light ground, often in a single contrasting color.

color_guidance.reason: Single-color pictorial printing on a light ground is a strong recognition convention, but historical examples use multiple ink colors and subjects.

patterns.qualification: Toile de Jouy is a textile and printing/design tradition associated with Jouy-en-Josas and pictorial printed cottons, not one fixed repeat or exclusively pastoral scene. The reference image is a representative recognition example only.

patterns.term_scope: printed cotton/textile tradition commonly associated with floral patterning
patterns.structure: Printed or painted cotton commonly presents dense flowers, foliage, branches, and other decorative motifs across the surface; glazed finishes are historically common.

color_guidance.reason: Multicolor floral imagery is a strong recognition convention, but chintz is not defined by one palette or one repeat.

patterns.qualification: Chintz is historically a cotton textile/material and printing or painting tradition, not one fixed floral motif. Modern visual discovery often uses the word for dense floral prints, so Pattern Dictionary keeps that usage explicitly qualified.

patterns.structure: Many small flowers or similarly small motifs are scattered across the ground, typically at a fine scale and without a dominant large bloom.

color_guidance.reason: Small-scale scattered floral density matters more than a particular colorway.

patterns.term_scope: modern floral surface-design family derived from Jacobean/crewelwork conventions

verified_names.ja: ジャコビアン・フローラル

patterns.structure: Scrolling stems carry stylized flowers, leaves, fruit, and sometimes animals or tree-like compositions in a dense ornamental arrangement.

color_guidance.reason: Botanical scroll structure and stylization are stronger identifiers than any fixed palette.

patterns.qualification: Jacobean Floral is a modern surface-design label derived from a broader historical Jacobean embroidery and crewelwork style, not one fixed motif. The reference repeat must represent characteristic scrolling botanical forms without claiming a universal Jacobean pattern.

patterns.term_scope: named dense field of many small flowers
patterns.structure: Numerous small flowering plants and blossoms densely fill the field so that the surface reads as a continuous flower-strewn ground.

color_guidance.reason: Dense multiplicity of small flowers is the core cue; historical palettes and media vary.

patterns.structure: Leaves, stems, flowers, seedpods, or other recognizable or abstracted plant forms organize the surface, ranging from naturalistic illustration to stylized repeats.

color_guidance.reason: Plant-form subject matter defines the family; palette and level of naturalism vary widely.

patterns.qualification: Botanical Print is a broad modern discovery label for plant-based imagery rather than one historically fixed motif or repeat. Sources support botanical forms as textile-pattern subject matter and current botanical-print usage, so the reference image is representative rather than canonical.

patterns.structure: Stylized serrated or jagged acanthus leaves curl outward in scrolling, symmetrical, or repeating ornamental compositions.

color_guidance.reason: Leaf form and ornamental curling define recognition; color depends on medium and period.

sources.publisher: Getty Research Institute, Art & Architecture Thesaurus

patterns.term_scope: generic framed circular or oval ornamental motif family
patterns.structure: Circular or oval framed units contain figures, flowers, geometry, or other ornament and may appear singly, centrally, or as a repeated field.

color_guidance.reason: The framed circular/oval ornament area defines the motif family; contents and colors vary.

sources.publisher: Getty Research Institute, Art & Architecture Thesaurus

patterns.structure: Recognizable lobed ivy leaves repeat alone or along stems and vines, often layered or trailing across the surface.

color_guidance.reason: Green supports immediate ivy recognition, but leaf silhouette and vine organization are the real cues and other palettes are valid.

patterns.qualification: Ivy Pattern is a broad botanical motif family, not one standardized repeat. The museum source verifies an ivy textile pattern and layered-leaf treatment, but Pattern Dictionary must not present that one arrangement as the universal ivy pattern.
